query: Earlier W-based high-entropy alloys showed promising microstructural stability, high-temperature strength, and irradiation tolerance, but most contained Nb, Mo, Cr, or Ni, whose activation behavior and other service limitations restrict their suitability for plasma-facing components. Candidate structural materials must combine thermal and mechanical performance with low neutron activation and rapid radioactive decay. The equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy uses refractory, relatively low-activation constituents and has shown creep and molten-salt-corrosion resistance, yet its plastic strain and toughness remain unreported and poorly understood. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs its plastic strain and toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing-component service? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to pure tungsten, the boundaries of validity, the cited prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.mechanism: Interaction between segregated alloying elements and dislocations, promoting grain boundary sliding deformation and enhancing plastic strain and toughness
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved plastic strain and toughness in the equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy compared to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing-component service conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of the plastic strain and toughness of the equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy with and without grain boundary engineering, under high-temperature plasma-facing-component service conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of elemental grain boundary segregation structures through grain boundary engineering does not result in improved plastic strain and toughness in the equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy compared to commercially used pure tungsten, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are novel high-temperature structural materials based on the design concept of high-entropy alloys (HEA) [, , ]. The multi-principal element characteristic of RHEAs leads to unique microstructures and remarkable properties, such as extremely high melting points, excellent high-temperature strengths, outstanding thermal stabilities, and exceptional creep, corrosion, and oxidation resistances [, , , ]. Owing to these advantages, RHEAs not only exhibit a significant application potential in aerospace and nuclear energy industries as high-temperature load-bearing or thermal protection structures, but also are regarded as an important development direction of high-temperature structural materials. Considering the crucial influence of microstructures on the properties, microstructure control is a meaningful approach to optimize and improve the macroscopic properties of alloys [,]. The element grain boundary segregation structure proposed in recent years provides extraordinary advantages to enhance the properties of alloys [,]. The interaction of segregated alloying elements and dislocation can enhance the hardness and strength of alloys. On the othe

Severe plastic deformation (SPD) is an effective approach to induce component element grain boundary segregation []. Both dislocations and defects generated during the deformation supply a driving force for the segregation behavior of solute atoms. The SPD techniques, such as surface mechanical grinding treatment and high-pressure torsion, have been successfully applied for Al and Mg alloys to obtain the grain boundary segregation structure and corresponding expected properties [,]. Notably, these methods are based on a considerable plasticity and acceptable deformation resistance at room temperature. However, for the ultrafine-grained RHEAs, the exceedingly high strength and limited ductility have brought considerable challenges to the SPD process. An increase in deformation temperature and reduction in strain rate are useful to improve the deformation performance. A higher temperature and lower strain rate are also conducive to a more adequate diffusion of solute atoms. Hence, based on the hot deformation technique and admissible plasticity of MoNbTaTiV RHEAs, the interaction between dislocation movement and multi-principal elemental atoms was used to obtain the grain boundary se

Ultrafine-grained MoNbTaTiV RHEAs were obtained via MA, spark plasma sintering, and hot deformation at various high temperatures and strain rates. With grain refinement and lattice strain increase, the large and inhomogeneous milled powder became refined and homogeneous after the MA. The component elements were segregated under relatively low temperatures and high strain rates. The fluctuation of element concentration occurred only near grain boundaries. The segregation gradually disappeared with the increase in deformation temperature and decrease in strain rate. The interaction between multi-principal elements and dislocation movement was responsible for component element segregation and determined the microhardness variations.

decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has focused on improving their mechanical properties, such as strength, ductility, and resistance to corrosion and irradiation. Recent studies have explored the effects of composition, processing, and microstructure on these properties. The trend suggests a shift towards designing alloys with optimized phase boundaries and grain structures to achieve enhanced performance.
decision.unsolved: The plastic strain and toughness of the equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy remain unreported and poorly understood, particularly under high-temperature plasma-facing-component service conditions. The underlying mechanisms governing these properties are not well established, and further research is needed to elucidate the relationships between composition, microstructure, and mechanical behavior.
decision.lever: investigating the effects of grain boundary engineering on plastic strain and toughness
decision.why: Given the recent findings on the importance of phase boundaries and grain structures in high-entropy alloys, a controlled experiment investigating the effects of grain boundary engineering on plastic strain and toughness in the WTaTiVZr alloy could provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms governing these properties. This approach could involve manipulating grain boundary characteristics, such as grain size, shape, and distribution, to observe their impact on mechanical behavior.
